Sampled HR@10 measures a different ranking problem from full-catalog HR@10: model orderings can reverse even after unlimited negative-sample repetitions. Repetition estimates sampling variability, not this bias ([Krichene–Rendle](https://ijcai.org/proceedings/2021/651)). A 2025 study explicitly assesses sampling reliability through resolution, fidelity, robustness and recovery of model rankings ([RecSys 2025](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086)). Keep the host’s fixed 99-negative validation unchanged; report supplementary candidate-resampling uncertainty separately from user-bootstrap uncertainty on those fixed candidates.

Popularity stratification has direct empirical support: a 2024 sequential-recommendation study finds aggregate metrics conceal head/mid/tail imbalances and negative-sampling tradeoffs ([Prakash et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276)). Proposed diagnostic design: report HR@10, target-rank distributions, sample counts and uncertainty by category, training-only target popularity and history length. Compare sampled versus full-catalog rankings on public training-history prefixes, explicitly labeling these as in-sample diagnostics; they cannot establish validation generalization. Rank diagnostics also avoid raw score-margin dependence on score scale.

Controlled perturbations can test probe sensitivity: RecSys 2024’s [Does It Look Sequential?](https://github.com/Antondfger/Does-It-Look-Sequential/) uses sequence shuffling and monitors HR@10, NDCG@10 and recommendation overlap. Extend this as a proposed sanity suite: shuffle nonpadding history, truncate recent context, and randomize scores without modifying official evaluation. Uniform random ranking among 100 candidates gives expected HR@10=0.10. These checks test whether probes respond to known damage; no located evidence establishes that they explain this benchmark’s four-category validation results. That requires measured comparisons across the actual NextItNet trials.
